The filing quantifies these costs in two places, and the figures are stated differently in each.

### 1. Total expected separation costs — MD&A, Part II, Item 7 ("Our Business and Strategy," printed p. 26)

> "We expect to incur costs of **approximately $700 million** in connection with separating Upjohn, of which, **approximately 75%** has been incurred since inception and through December 31, 2021. These charges include costs and expenses related to **separation of legal entities and transaction costs**."

- **$700 million** — total separation costs Pfizer expects to incur in connection with separating Upjohn (a forward-looking/expected figure).
- **75%** — the portion already incurred "since inception and through December 31, 2021."
- Scope per this passage: separation of legal entities and transaction costs.

### 2. Separation-related costs actually incurred — Note 2B, "Divestitures — Upjohn Separation and Combination with Mylan" (printed p. 65)

> "As a result of the separation of Upjohn, we incurred separation-related costs of **$434 million in 2020** and **$83 million in 2019**, which are included in *Discontinued operations—net of tax*. These costs primarily relate to **professional fees for regulatory filings and separation activities within finance, tax, legal and information system functions as well as investment banking fees**."

- **$434 million** — separation-related costs incurred in **2020** (the year of the spin-off/Combination), reported in *Discontinued operations—net of tax*.
- **$83 million** — separation-related costs incurred in **2019** (pre-separation planning), also in *Discontinued operations—net of tax*.
- Composition per this note: professional fees for regulatory filings; separation activities in finance, tax, legal and information system functions; and investment banking fees.

### How the two relate
The $434 million (2020) and $83 million (2019) are the incurred amounts that make up the ~75% of the ~$700 million expected total as of December 31, 2021 (i.e., roughly $525 million). The $700 million is an aggregate expected total covering both the pre-separation (2019) and post-separation (2020–2021) periods; the $434 million / $83 million split is the incurred-by-year breakdown for 2020 and 2019 only, since the filing does not state a separate 2021 separation-cost amount.

### Related but distinct items (to avoid conflation)
- **$152 million** (2019), in *Other (income)/deductions—net* (Note 4): charges for "external incremental costs, such as transaction costs and costs to separate our Consumer Healthcare business into a separate legal entity" associated with the **GSK Consumer Healthcare JV** — a different transaction, not Upjohn.

- Because these separation charges sit in *Discontinued operations—net of tax*, they are removed in the non-GAAP Adjusted income reconciliation ($585 million in 2021, $2,879 million in 2020, $6,056 million in 2019).

**Source document:** NVDA_2024_10K.pdf (NVIDIA's fiscal 2024 Form 10-K, filed February 21, 2024)

| Item | FY2024 amount | Source |
|---|---|---|

The $2.2 billion total was identical in fiscal 2023 (excluded here); the release rose to $540 million from $137 million in fiscal 2023 (also excluded). The filing states the net effect was an unfavorable gross-margin impact of 2.7% in fiscal 2024 (percentage excluded per your instruction).

### The two components of the $2.2 billion (Note 10 footnotes)

1. **$774 million** — "an inventory provision of $774 million ... in cost of revenue" (Note 10, footnote 1 to the Inventories table, p. 68). This is the write-down of inventory to the lower of cost or net realizable value for **obsolete or excess inventory**.

### Accounting policy context

- **Note 1, Inventories (p. 58):** "We charge cost of sales for inventory provisions to write-down our inventory to the lower of cost or net realizable value or for obsolete or excess inventory, and for excess product purchase commitments." Once written down, inventory "creates a new cost basis ... that is not subsequently written-up." NVIDIA also records "a liability for noncancelable purchase commitments with suppliers for quantities in excess of our future demand forecasts."
- **Critical Accounting Estimates — Inventories (MD&A, p. 37):** most provisions relate to excess quantities of products/components, based on inventory levels and future purchase commitments compared with assumptions about future demand and market conditions.
- **PwC Critical Audit Matter (p. 49):** "Valuation of Inventories – Provisions for Excess or Obsolete Inventories and Excess Product Purchase Commitments" was the sole critical audit matter, citing significant management judgment on future demand and market conditions.

NVIDIA's fiscal 2026 Form 10-K (year ended January 25, 2026) explains the complexity of valuing non-marketable equity securities in three places: the Critical Accounting Estimates section of MD&A (p. 38), the significant accounting policies in Note 1 (p. 60), Note 8 (pp. 66-67), and Item 7A's market risk discussion (p. 45). Taken together, the reasons given are:

**1. The investments are in private companies with no readily determinable fair value.** Note 1 states that non-marketable equity securities "consist of investments in privately-held companies that do not have a readily determinable fair value." There is no quoted market price and no active market in which identical or similar interests trade, so fair value cannot be observed directly.

**2. Lack of readily available market data and observable transactions.** Item 7A is the most explicit statement: "Valuations of our non-marketable equity securities are inherently complex due to the lack of readily available market data and observable transactions, and impact of macroeconomic factors."

**3. Inherent lack of liquidity.** Note 1 ties the need for judgment directly to this: fair value is "based upon observable inputs in an inactive market and the valuation requires our judgment due to the absence of market prices and inherent lack of liquidity."

**4. The measurement alternative forces reliance on unobservable inputs.** Because the securities are carried at cost minus impairment, if any, and adjusted only for observable price changes in orderly transactions for an identical or similar investment in the same issuer, the carrying amounts are not marked to a quoted price. The resulting adjustments "may require use of unobservable inputs" (MD&A). Note 8 lists the specific unobservable inputs NVIDIA uses: volatility, expected time to liquidity, risk-free rate, and security-specific rights and obligations.

**5. Impairment testing is inherently judgmental.** NVIDIA assesses impairment quarterly "based on qualitative and quantitative factors, including the investee's operating performance and market trends" (MD&A), and Note 1 adds that impairment is assessed on "quantitative and qualitative factors," with any identified impairment written down to fair value through Other income, net.

**6. Macroeconomic conditions feed into the valuation.** Item 7A identifies macroeconomic factors as one of the three drivers of valuation complexity, alongside the data and transaction gaps above.

**Context on materiality:** the estimate is significant for fiscal 2026. ### 1. The COVID-19 pandemic's severe initial impact on commercial aviation

The charges were triggered by the pandemic. The filing states that "the initial effects of the COVID-19 pandemic on commercial airlines and aircraft manufacturers were particularly severe," and in Note 13 that Berkshire reevaluated certain reporting units "due to the disruptions arising from the COVID-19 pandemic, which we believed most significantly affected the air travel, commercial aerospace and supporting industries."

### 2. Specific industry information considered in the reevaluation

Berkshire says that in the second quarter of 2020 it "quantitatively reevaluated goodwill for impairment for certain reporting units, and most significantly for PCC," considering, "including but not limited to":

- **Announcements by airlines concerning potential future demand, employment levels and aircraft orders**;
- **Announcements by manufacturers of reduced aircraft production**; and
- **The actions Berkshire was taking or might take in the future to restructure operations.**

### 3. The resulting valuation changes: higher discount rates and lower cash-flow forecasts

"Consequently, we deemed it prudent under the prevailing circumstances to **increase discount rates and reduce prior long-term forecasts of future cash flows** for purposes of reviewing for impairments." Note 13 adds that the charges "were determined based on discounted cash flow methods and reflected our assessments of the risks and uncertainties associated with the aerospace industry."

### 4. Fair value falling below carrying value (the mechanical trigger)

Under the policy in Note 1(n), if a reporting unit's carrying amount (including goodwill) exceeds its estimated fair value, the excess is charged to earnings; for indefinite-lived intangibles, the excess of carrying value over fair value is charged to earnings. The reevaluation therefore produced charges of **$10.0 billion of goodwill** (Note 13's rollforward shows $10,033 million) and **$638 million of indefinite-lived intangible assets**, of which **approximately $10 billion related to PCC**, whose pre-charge carrying values of goodwill and indefinite-lived intangibles were approximately **$31 billion** (goodwill ~$17 billion and indefinite-lived intangibles ~$14 billion), substantially all recorded in connection with Berkshire's 2016 acquisition of PCC.

### 5. A judgment call made under uncertainty

Berkshire frames the decision as one of prudence rather than certainty, noting it "deemed it prudent under the prevailing circumstances" to make the changes. Note 1(b) explains that "the extent of the effects over longer terms on the demand for certain of our products and services cannot be reasonably estimated at this time," and that "significant estimates used in the preparation of our financial statements including those associated with evaluations of certain long-lived assets, goodwill and other intangible assets for impairment... may be subject to significant adjustments in future periods." The 2020 charge was also disclosed in the "Other" results of operations as an after-tax $9.8 billion charge attributable to impairments of goodwill and certain identifiable intangible assets recorded in connection with the PCC acquisition (total after-tax goodwill and intangible asset impairments of $10,381 million for 2020, versus none in 2021).

### 6. Corroborating operating facts at PCC during 2020

MD&A on industrial products (page K-49) describes the operating deterioration behind the valuation change: PCC's 2020 revenues fell $3.0 billion (28.9%) to $7.3 billion and pre-tax earnings fell 64.5% to $650 million, as "the COVID-19 pandemic contributed to material declines in commercial air travel and aircraft production"; airlines "delaying delivery of aircraft orders or, in some cases, cancelling aircraft orders, resulting in significant reductions in build rates by aircraft manufacturers"; Boeing 737 MAX production issues "contributed to the declines in aerospace product sales across the industry"; and PCC took "aggressive restructuring actions to resize operations," reducing its worldwide workforce by about 40% and recording approximately $295 million of restructuring, inventory and fixed asset charges in 2020.

### 7. Subsequent developments confirming the reset

In the fourth-quarter 2021 annual review, Berkshire again concluded no impairment was required, but disclosed that the estimated fair values of five reporting units did not exceed carrying values by at least 20%. PCC's estimated fair value was approximately **$34.5 billion** versus a carrying value of approximately **$31.1 billion** (a 10.7% cushion, including ~$7.5 billion of goodwill), and four other reporting units had an aggregate fair value of ~$2.5 billion versus ~$2.3 billion of carrying value (9.2% cushion, including ~$1.2 billion of goodwill). **In summary:** the filing attributes the charges to the severe initial COVID-19 disruption of commercial aviation and aerospace, the resulting collapse in airline demand, aircraft orders and manufacturer build rates, and the associated restructuring actions at PCC; to Berkshire's judgment that, under the prevailing circumstances, it was prudent to raise discount rates and lower long-term cash-flow forecasts; and to the resulting conclusion, based on discounted cash flow methods, that the fair value of PCC's reporting unit and indefinite-lived intangibles had fallen below their carrying values.

Under the risk factor "We may not realize the anticipated benefits of mergers, acquisitions, joint ventures/strategic alliances or divestitures," Boeing states that "difficulties in integrating Spirit may result in the failure to realize anticipated benefits of the acquisition (**including anticipated synergies and safety and quality improvements**) in the expected timeframe or at all, as well as operational challenges, the diversion of management's attention from other ongoing business concerns, and unforeseen expenses." Boeing also notes it must provide services to buyers of divested Spirit businesses (including Airbus) under transitional/longer-term services agreements, and that nonperformance of those obligations could harm its business.

### Synergies expected to be concentrated in Commercial Airplanes (Note 2, p. 76)

Provisional goodwill of **$9,997 million** was assigned to the **BCA segment "as we expect the majority of synergies from the Spirit Acquisition to relate to the commercial airplane segment."** This is the filing's only indication of where the synergy benefits are expected to accrue.

### What the transaction brings in (MD&A Overview, p. 27)

Boeing describes the acquisition as encompassing **all of Spirit's Boeing-related commercial operations** — fuselages for the 737, P-8 and KC-46 Tanker programs, and major structures for the 767, 777 and 787 programs — plus **Spirit's defense and aftermarket businesses** and portions of Spirit's operations in **Belfast, Ireland**. Spirit employs approximately **15,000 people**. It was structured as a share exchange of approximately $4.7 billion of Boeing stock, with Boeing also paying off certain Spirit debt and obligations and assuming the remainder.

The safety/quality benefit rationale connects to the January 2024 737-9 door-plug accident: Item 1 (Regulatory Matters, p. 6) notes that the FAA "investigated the 737 quality control system, **including Spirit AeroSystems Holdings, Inc. (Spirit)**, and increased its oversight of our production and quality and safety management systems." Item 1A further states that the Spirit Acquisition, alongside the production slowdowns, "significantly impacted our financial position, results of operations and cash flows" in the context of production-system health (p. 10). The 10-K also notes the acquisition added $131 million to product warranty liabilities (Note 15, p. 92).

Notably, the 10-K does **not** contain a fuller strategic-rationale discussion (e.g., quantified cost synergies, supply-chain vertical-integration savings, or aftermarket/revenue-growth targets). ## Boeing's 2024 Form 10-K (BA_2024_10K.pdf) — causes it links to lower 2024 commercial airplane deliveries

**Context from the filing:** BCA deliveries (including intercompany deliveries) fell to **348 in 2024 from 528 in 2023** — 737: 265 vs. 396; 747: 0 vs. 1; 767: 18 vs. 32; 777: 14 vs. 26; 787: 51 vs. 73 (MD&A, Commercial Airplanes Results of Operations).

### The causes the filing expressly links to deliveries — eight in total

1. **The IAM 751 work stoppage (strike).** This is the filing's most explicit delivery statement: "The IAM 751 work stoppage significantly reduced aircraft deliveries in the second half of 2024." The strike (Sept. 13 – Nov. 4, 2024) paused production of the 737, 767, 777 and 777X (only 787 in Charleston continued); production resumed in December 2024, leaving too little of the year to recover the lost deliveries. *(Overview, MD&A; also Human Capital and Risk Factors.)*

2. **Post–Alaska Airlines 737-9 accident safety and quality actions.** The FAA grounded and required inspections of all 737-9s, investigated the 737 quality control system (including Spirit), increased oversight, and said it would not approve 737 production rate increases beyond 38/month or additional production lines. Boeing "slowed production rates and delayed planned production rate increases." The filing ties this directly to deliveries in the cash flow discussion: commercial airplane cash outflows reflect "slowed and/or paused production **and lower deliveries** as a result of ongoing safety and quality improvement actions the Company is taking following the Alaska Airlines accident." All 737-9 aircraft in production also had to pass the enhanced inspection process before delivery. *(MD&A Overview; Program Highlights; Cash Flow Summary.)*

3. **Supply chain constraints, supplier quality issues and labor instability.** The same cash flow sentence links lower deliveries to "supply chain constraints." In the Program Highlights, Boeing slowed 787 production to below 5 per month "due to supply chain constraints as well as other production issues," and for the 767, "we experienced factory disruption, including supply chain delays and quality issues." MD&A states Boeing and its suppliers face "supply chain disruptions as a result of production quality issues, global supply chain constraints, and labor instability," which "reduced overall productivity." *(MD&A Business Environment and Trends; Program Highlights; Cash Flow Summary.)*

4. **737-7 and 737-10 certification delays and the unresolved engine anti-ice engineering solution.** Boeing remained "working through the certification process of the 737-7 and 737-10 models, which have been delayed, while we work through the engineering solution for the engine anti-ice system." About 35 737-7/-10 aircraft sat in inventory at year-end 2024 because they could not be certified and delivered. *(737 Program Highlights.)*

5. **777X certification and flight-test delays.** "Based on flight test delays and our revised assessment of certification timelines, the anticipated first delivery of the 777-9 was delayed to 2026 and the 777-8 Freighter moved to 2028," with first 777-8 passenger delivery not before 2030; flight testing was paused from August 2024 to January 2025; and the decision to slow the 777X production rate ramp "resulted in higher production costs and further customer delivery delays." *(777/777X Program Highlights; also Critical Accounting Estimates.)*

6. **787 business class seat delays.** "Delays associated with business class seats adversely impacted 2024 deliveries and will continue to impact deliveries in 2025." *(787 Program Highlights.)*

7. **787 prior-year inventory requiring rework.** About 25 aircraft produced prior to 2023 remained in inventory pending inspection/rework ($256 million expensed as abnormal production costs); Boeing expects to complete the rework and deliver the majority in 2025 — so those deliveries fell out of 2024. *(787 Program Highlights; Note 8.)*

8. **The 767 freighter program end decision and the resulting accounting quantity reductions.** Boeing decided to end 767 freighter production (now late 2026/early 2027), reducing the 767 accounting quantity by 9 units in Q3 2024 and 7 units in Q4 2024. Because the accounting quantity is "the estimated quantity of airplanes that will be produced for delivery," these reductions directly cut the number of 767s available to deliver. *(767 Program Highlights; Backlog/Accounting Quantity discussion.)*

**Minor, non-narrative item:** the 747 program was completed in Q4 2022 and the last aircraft was delivered in February 2023, which mechanically accounts for the 747 delivery falling from 1 to 0.

### Causes deliberately excluded as cost/revenue/rate-only, not delivery-linked

- **The $4,079 million of 777X and 767 reach-forward losses** and the related $443 million 737-9 customer considerations charge (reflected as a reduction of Sales of products). The 737-9 consideration is a revenue/concession effect tied to the grounding disruption (largely liquidated "by lower customer delivery payments"), and the reach-forward losses are earnings charges; the filing does not cite them as causes of the 2024 delivery shortfall.
- **The new IAM 751 contract's pay increases and non-union pay enhancements** — cited as pressuring margins, costs and cash flows, not deliveries.
- **Lower abnormal production costs ($1,271 million favorable), higher R&D, and margin compression** — cost/revenue drivers only.
- **The FAA's 38-per-month rate cap and related rate-increase delays** stand alone as a rate constraint, though here they form part of cause #2, which the filing does connect to lower deliveries.

**Bottom line:** Boeing's 2024 Form 10-K links its lower 2024 commercial airplane deliveries to **eight causes**: the IAM 751 strike; the post-737-9-accident safety and quality actions (slowed/paused production, FAA oversight and the 38/month cap, 737-9 grounding and pre-delivery inspections); supply chain constraints and supplier quality issues; 737-7/-10 certification delays and the anti-ice engineering solution; 777X certification and flight-test delays; 787 business class seat delays; 787 rework inventory; and the 767 production-end decision and accounting quantity contractions.

Based on Berkshire Hathaway's 2024 Form 10-K (BRK_2024_10K.pdf), the filing gives the following reasons for evaluating BHE on an after-tax basis rather than a pre-tax basis.

### The explicit reason stated in the segment footnote (Note 26, p. K-109)

The clearest statement appears in Note 26, "Business segment data," where Berkshire describes how its chief operating decision maker evaluates the businesses:

> "For most non-insurance businesses, pre-tax earnings are considered in allocating resources and capital, **although income taxes are also considered at BHE, given the magnitude of production tax credits associated with wind-powered electricity generation investments and the related impacts from regulation.**"

So the stated reason is twofold: (1) the sheer magnitude of the production tax credits from wind-powered generation, and (2) the regulatory consequences flowing from those credits.

### The MD&A framing (p. K-43)

The BHE discussion in Management's Discussion and Analysis opens with:

> "The discussion of BHE's operating results that follows is based on after-tax earnings, **reflecting how the energy businesses are managed and evaluated.**"

Accordingly, BHE is presented on an after-tax basis (net earnings of $4,163 million in 2024; $4,026 million attributable to BHE; $3,730 million attributable to Berkshire shareholders), with the segment discussion broken out by after-tax lines for U.S. utilities, natural gas pipelines, other energy businesses, real estate brokerage, and "corporate interest and other" — the last being described as "after-tax earnings" that "include BHE corporate interest expense and unallocated corporate and income tax expenses."

### Supporting reasons evident elsewhere in the filing

**1. Pre-tax earnings are an actively misleading measure for BHE because of the tax credits.** BHE's effective income tax rate is negative and volatile because production tax credits from wind-powered electricity generation exceed its pre-tax income: an income tax *benefit* of $1,871 million in 2024 (effective rate **(81.6)%**), $2,022 million in 2023 (**(215.1)%**), and $1,629 million in 2022 (**(51.8)%**). The MD&A table footnotes the line: "* Includes significant production tax credits primarily from wind-powered electricity generation." Note 20 confirms that "U.S. income tax credits derive primarily from production tax credits associated with wind-energy generation of BHE." Consequently, 2024 pre-tax earnings of $2,292 million convert to net earnings after income taxes of $4,163 million — the two measures tell very different stories, so an after-tax view is the meaningful one.

**2. Income taxes are a direct, recoverable component of BHE's regulated rates.** The MD&A states that "the rates BHE's regulated businesses charge customers for energy and services are **largely based on the costs of business operations, including income taxes and a return on capital**, and are subject to regulatory approval," and that to the extent such costs are not allowed in approved rates, operating results will be adversely affected. Because income taxes are embedded in the rate-setting formula, the tax effects are an integral, recurring part of the economics of the business rather than a below-the-line adjustment that can be ignored when judging performance.

**3. The tax credits and their regulatory impacts are recognized over time through rates, not as a one-off.** Under Note 1(t), "Regulated utilities and energy businesses," certain costs are deferred as regulatory assets and certain income accrued as regulatory liabilities, subsequently amortized into operating expenses and revenues over various future periods, with continued assessment of probable future inclusion in regulated rates. Thus the wind production tax credits are spread through rates over the lives of the related assets and projects, making after-tax earnings the measure that corresponds to how the business actually earns and recovers value.

**4. Evaluating on pre-tax would obscure the drivers of year-to-year changes.** The 2024 discussions turn on after-tax items — e.g., the $157 million of comparative income tax benefits from recognized wind production tax credits at the U.S. utilities, lower income tax expense at Northern Powergrid from 2023 U.K. Energy Profits Levy charges, higher effective tax rates at the natural gas pipelines following the September 1, 2023 acquisition of an additional 50% limited partner interest in Cove Point, and lower earnings from wind tax equity investments. ### Bottom line

The filing's stated rationale is that BHE is unique among Berkshire's non-insurance businesses in the **magnitude of production tax credits from its wind-powered electricity generation investments and the related regulatory impacts of those credits**. Because income taxes are embedded in BHE's regulated cost-of-service rates and the credits are recovered through rates over time, taxes are not a peripheral item for BHE but a core, integral component of how the business is managed, evaluated, and generates returns. That, in the filing's words, is why "the discussion of BHE's operating results that follows is based on after-tax earnings."
